one-line thesis: Shadowfax delivered record profitability (PAT INR 112cr FY26, +17x YoY) driven by operating leverage and mix shift to high-margin D2C/Vertical QC, while aggressively expanding asset-heavy sortation capacity and launching a 100-dark-store strategy for vertical quick commerce to capture the next wave of digital penetration.
financial scorecard: Revenue: INR 1,237cr (Q4, +74% YoY, +6.7% QoQ); FY26 Rev: INR 4,200cr (+69% YoY). EBITDA: INR 58cr (Q4, 4.7% margin vs 4.3% Q3, 0.7% YoY); FY26 Adj EBITDA: INR 159cr (~3x FY25). PAT: INR 56cr (Q4, 4.5% margin); FY26 PAT: INR 112cr vs INR 6cr FY25. Order Book: Not disclosed (flow business). Net Debt: Not explicitly stated; Capex funded via ops/cash. One-offs: Dual running costs for new sortation centers (e.g., OneNCR) and rapid real estate expansion (35% increase in space Sep-Mar) temporarily suppress margins despite record profitability.
guidance: Revenue Growth: 27-30% overall (FY27); Hyperlocal: 45-50% YoY. Margin: 100-120 bps expansion annually until FY28, then 200-250 bps/year to reach early double-digit steady-state EBITDA. Order Inflow: Targeting 17,000 pin codes by FY27 end (from 15,600). Capex: INR 180-190cr for FY27 (flat YoY absolute), with <10% allocated to dark stores; majority in sortation automation.
order book & pipeline: N/A (Transaction-based logistics flow); Key metric is volume growth and pin code coverage (15,600 currently, targeting 17,000 by FY27 end).
segment / subsidiary detail: Express Parcel (75% of rev): Gaining share from inefficient 3PLs and insourced arms; D2C/SME segment growing 2.5x YoY with 15-20% higher pricing. Hyperlocal: +50% YoY, +16% QoQ; onboarded Amazon Now; focusing on vertical QC. Other Logistics: INR 80cr (wind-down of low-value experiments complete, pivoting to critical logistics via CriticaLog).
growth verticals / optionality: 1) D2C/SME direct onboarding (Shadowfax 360) targeting 15-16 lakh sellers. 2) Large shipment capability (white goods) expanding to 10,000 pin codes. 3) Vertical Quick Commerce: Setting up 100 dark stores in FY27 for specialized categories (grocery, fashion, hardware) with 30-45 min delivery. 4) AI adoption reducing technical barriers for SMEs and optimizing routing/utilization.
margins & cost dynamics: Q4 EBITDA margin 4.7%; FY26 PAT margin 4.5%. Cost structure: ~50% partner expense (crowdsourced), ~18-19% trucking, <10% fuel (pass-through via surcharge). Margin expansion driven by mix shift to high-margin D2C/Vertical QC and operating leverage from automated sortation centers. Current drag from dual-running costs during facility transitions (6-8 months ramp).
capex / expansion: FY26 Capex: ~4.5% of revenue. FY27 Guidance: INR 180-190cr (absolute flat vs FY26). Allocation: >60% in sortation centers over last 3 years; 85% in sortation + last mile hubs. Dark stores <10% of FY27 capex. Strategy: Asset-heavy under roof (automation), asset-light on road.
capital allocation: Prioritizing organic capacity expansion (sortation automation, dark stores) and geographic penetration (120-150 new pin codes/month). Acquired 100% of CriticaLog (high-value logistics) for integration. No dividend/buyback mentioned; reinvestment mode for 10x scale.
risks & watch-items: 1) Geopolitical volatility impacting crude/fuel prices (mitigated by surcharge). 2) Execution risk in scaling 100 dark stores and integrating vertical QC clients. 3) Intense competition in quick commerce leading to pricing pressure (though mgmt cites fragmented client base reduces single-client leverage). 4) Ramp-up period costs for new facilities impacting short-term margins.
management quality / tone: Highly confident and aggressive; emphasizing 'phenomenal tailwinds,' 'record profitability,' and 'audacious bets' on vertical QC and AI. Tone suggests inflection point where early capex investments are beginning to yield operating leverage.
non-obvious takeaways: 1) Shift from horizontal to vertical quick commerce as the primary growth lever, with Shadowfax positioning as the natural 3PL for capital-constrained vertical players. 2) AI is not just an efficiency tool but a demand generator by lowering technical barriers for SMEs to go online. 3) Network design philosophy: Fewer, larger last-mile nodes to optimize transportation mesh, contrary to industry trend of hyper-fragmented nodes. 4) Dual-running costs for 6-8 months per new facility create a temporary margin drag that masks true steady-state profitability.

themes.title: Logistics, ports & supply-chain formalization
themes.need: E-commerce, quick-commerce and GST-driven warehousing consolidation plus a 1P->3P shift drive an integrated-logistics up-cycle. DELHIVERY hit early FCF (>1B parcels, Express +46% rev) with Express targeting 16-18% margin; CONCOR/GATEWAY/JSWINFRA on rail/ports; ALLCARGO/MAHLOG/TVSSCS/VRLLOG on 3PL/road; BLUEDART/TCIEXP/WCIL/SNOWMAN on express + cold-chain; DELHIVERY/SHADOWFAX on quick-commerce fulfilment. Q1FY27's clearest turnaround datapoint: MAHLOG swung to a +INR 25.4cr PAT from a -INR 10.8cr loss on +23% revenue, with B2B Express (Rivigo) gross margin turning +6% from -3.8% and its EBITDA loss cut to -INR 1.6cr from -INR 11.8cr, guided to EBITDA breakeven within FY27, while Contract Logistics grew 26% with margin diluted only ~46bps on new-site start-up costs (opening a site almost every week).
themes.driver: Express/quick-commerce volume momentum; warehousing leasing; port/rail throughput; operating-leverage inflection.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Shadowfax Technologies is a technology-led third-party logistics provider for India's digital commerce, having expanded its express-market share from approximately 8% in FY 22 to an estimated 27-29% by the fourth quarter of FY 26.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Shadowfax Technologies Limited is a new-age, technology-led third-party logistics (3PL) company that leverages technology to facilitate the penetration of digital commerce in India, operating across three service lines: Express, Hyperlocal and Other logistics services. Express covers forward parcel delivery plus value-added services (reverse pickups, hand-in-hand exchange, and prime same-day and next-day delivery); Hyperlocal covers quick-commerce fulfilment, food and on-demand delivery and mobility services in high-density consumption centres; Other logistics services include critical (high-value) logistics through CriticaLog, strategic insourcing of unbundled services and dark-store operations. It serves horizontal and non-horizontal e-commerce marketplaces, quick commerce platforms, food delivery and on-demand mobility platforms, D2C brands and SMEs, with substantially all last-mile deliveries executed through a crowdsourced gig delivery-partner network.

cost_leadership.title: Supply chain integration (RHP report)
cost_leadership.body: Asset-light, fully leased model across logistics facilities and linehaul while retaining ownership of automation and machinery for operational control. Integrated network spans first-mile pick-up and return-to-origin centers, middle-mile sorting, last-mile delivery and linehaul (more than 3,000 leased trucks daily, all leased from third-party fleet partners), interconnected via a hybrid mesh-based linehaul network with dynamic routing. Last mile is executed through a crowdsourced gig-based delivery partner fleet (205,864 Average Quarterly Unique Transacting Delivery Partners for six months ended September 30, 2025, across more than 2,300 cities) plus franchisee partners on a variable cost model; India's largest crowdsourced last-mile delivery fleet among 3PL e-commerce players (RedSeer). Partnerships with OEMs provide delivery partners access to EVs on a rental basis via a three-way EV marketplace (delivery partners, OEMs, quick-commerce clients); airline partnerships enable next-day delivery in metropolitan cities. Proprietary in-house technology stack (supply-demand allocation engine, Frodo delivery-partner lifecycle system with UIDAI/NSDL touchless onboarding, SF Shield fraud detection with track-and-trace, SF Maps address intelligence, APIs for client integration) orchestrates the network. Forward extension into multi-brand dark store operations and strategic insourcing of unbundled supply-chain services; acquisition of 89.59% of Criticalog India Private Limited (November 22, 2024) added freight management, air and road express, freight forwarding, intermodal transportation, warehousing, customs house clearance, trade compliance and supply chain management capabilities.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural under-penetration of Indian e-commerce: it contributed only about 7.6% of retail in FY 26 against roughly 32% in China and 19% in the USA, with just 3-4 e-commerce shipments per capita versus 75-85 in China and 60-70 in the USA; industry estimates suggest online retail penetration could roughly double towards approximately 14% over the coming five years.
- Online retail is projected to grow at a CAGR of 20-25% between FY 25 and FY 30, with India's per-capita e-commerce spend at just 1-2% of per-capita income against 8-10% in China and 3-5% in the USA.
- Shipment volumes are growing faster than e-commerce value as lower average-order-value categories (fashion, beauty, personal care) expand and tier-2 and smaller cities contribute a rising share - mirroring the trajectory seen in more mature markets such as China.
- Quick commerce is the fastest-growing category, expanding at 50-62%, while D2C brands and vertical, category-focused platforms extend the market beyond traditional horizontal marketplaces.
- Shift to organised 3PL: organised providers catered to an estimated 40-42% of e-commerce shipments in FY 26, with outsourcing intensity varying widely by sub-segment (higher for non-horizontal and niche platforms, still nascent in quick commerce), leaving considerable headroom; the limited profitability of captive logistics arms is expected to favour outsourcing.
- Market consolidation around a few scaled national operators is improving structural economics for the leading players - though large-platform insourcing creates near-term volatility.
- Gig workforce supply: an estimated 10 million-plus gig workers today, projected to reach approximately 24 million (about 4% of the workforce) by FY 30, enabling flexible, variable-cost last-mile networks.
- Enterprises increasingly seek partners offering integrated first-mile, mid-mile and last-mile, warehousing and technology solutions on a total-cost basis, favouring players with deep national capabilities.
- Technology and AI are improving routing, sortation, forecasting and cost efficiency across the industry and are expected to unlock further productivity gains and new demand.
- Government initiatives - Bharatmala, PM Gati Shakti, the National Logistics Policy and digitisation such as FASTag, e-way bills and digital fuel cards - continue to lower logistics costs and drive formalisation.
- Macro backdrop: India remained the fastest-growing major economy in FY 26 with real GDP estimated to have grown by approximately 7.7% and average CPI inflation around 2.1%; at its June 2026 review the RBI kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, lowered its FY 27 real GDP projection to 6.6% (from 6.9%) and raised its CPI projection to 5.1% (from 4.6%).
- Global backdrop: the IMF projects global growth to moderate to 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027 with headline inflation rising to about 4.4% in 2026; the late-February 2026 Middle East conflict disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and spiked energy prices, which remain above pre-conflict levels despite de-escalation.
- Threats flagged: volatile fuel and input costs (fuel is a major component of transportation cost, with fuel-price and wage inflation amplified by geopolitical events); infrastructure gaps in road, telecommunications, internet and air-cargo; and any slowdown in economic or consumption growth or a shift of consumption to alternate channels.
- Management's central thesis: as a model-agnostic platform serving deliveries from ten minutes to several days, the company is positioned to be a primary beneficiary as digital penetration rises by an estimated 120-150 basis points each year towards approximately 14% by FY 30.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Shadowfax is an asset-light 3PL whose expansion is network build-out rather than plant capacity. Its stated architecture has three components: 'under the roof - asset heavy', where every last-mile hub, sortation centre and dark store is self-operated, run by its own employees and equipped with state-of-the-art automation; an 'optimised node count' of deliberately fewer, larger, high-capacity last-mile facilities rather than many small ones; and 'on the road - asset-light', where the company does not own the trucks used for its operations, keeping transportation cost variable. Over the last three years more than 60% of all capex has gone into sortation centres specifically, and sortation centres plus last-mile facilities together have absorbed 85% of all capex. FY 26 total capex was 185 Cr (4.4% of revenue), of which 69% was deployed in network and automation; depreciation commentary attributes the increase mainly to higher right-of-use asset depreciation as the leased network of sort centres and last-mile facilities expanded, alongside higher depreciation on property, plant and equipment following the FY 26 capital expenditure of 185 crore. The milestone of the year was the commissioning of OneNCR, one of India's largest automated sort centres, with a designed throughput of approximately 48,000 packages per hour (described elsewhere in the report as processing 10 lakh daily orders), significantly strengthening sorting capacity. The network reached 15,656 pin codes and 4,778 first-mile, middle-mile and last-mile touchpoints with over 47 lakh square feet of operational space as at 31 March 2026, up from 13,169 pin codes and 3,093 touchpoints in FY 24 and 14,387 pin codes and 3,964 touchpoints in FY 25, with 120-150 new pin codes opened per month and 3,500+ trucks running on a daily basis. The 1,000 crore primary capital raised at the January 2026 listing is being deployed across four stated buckets: sortation centre expansion (investment in owned, automated sort centres including OneNCR); pin code coverage, expanding reach from 15,656 to a target of 17,000 pin codes by FY 27 and full national coverage by FY 28; the Shadowfax 360 D2C and SME self-serve platform; and dark stores for vertical quick commerce, with 100 dark stores to be set up in FY 27. Inorganic expansion during the year comprised the completed acquisition of Criticalog India Private Limited, extending the company into critical and high-value logistics. Automation was also expanded across the logistics infrastructure through deployment of advanced sortation systems at the sort centres, and the Frodo partner platform handles digital onboarding, AI-driven order allocation, earnings tracking and performance management for a crowdsourced fleet of 2.6 lakh-plus quarterly active delivery partners (average quarterly unique transacting delivery partners of 2,31,345 in FY 26, versus 1,51,385 in FY 25 and 1,01,761 in FY 24).

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Highly confident and aggressive; emphasizing 'phenomenal tailwinds,' 'record profitability,' and 'audacious bets' on vertical QC and AI. Tone suggests inflection point where early capex investments are beginning to yield operating leverage.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Variable-cost crowdsourced last-mile: 100% of last-mile deliveries executed through what is among India's largest crowdsourced gig delivery-partner networks, averaging over 2.31 lakh unique transacting delivery partners per quarter in FY 26, where a single partner can fulfil e-commerce, food and quick-commerce orders on one app
- Asset-right network architecture: leased facilities and a leased linehaul fleet paired with in-house automation, with everything 'under the roof' (last-mile facilities, sortation centres and dark stores) self-operated and progressively automated while everything 'on the road' stays variable
- Market leadership: market leader in reverse-pickup, same-day delivery and 3PL quick-commerce solutions, and the fastest-growing 3PL company of scale in India
- Scale of coverage: network reached 15,656 pin codes supported by 4,778 touchpoints and more than 47 lakh square feet of operational space as at 31 March 2026
- Proprietary in-house technology stack with embedded AI - systems for supply-demand allocation, address intelligence and geo-coding, fraud detection and prevention, and shipment security and traceability
- Automation depth: OneNCR, among India's largest automated sort centres, with a designed throughput of approximately 48,000 packages per hour
- Breadth of portfolio allowing the most diverse and complex client needs to be addressed from a single, integrated platform, spanning deliveries from ten minutes to several days
- Demonstrated operating leverage: adjusted EBITDA positivity maintained for 11 consecutive quarters by the time of listing, with total operating expenses easing to 96.2% of revenue from operations in FY 26 from 98.0% in FY 25
- Well-capitalised and near debt-free balance sheet following the January 2026 IPO primary raise

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: 1) Geopolitical volatility impacting crude/fuel prices (mitigated by surcharge). 2) Execution risk in scaling 100 dark stores and integrating vertical QC clients. 3) Intense competition in quick commerce leading to pricing pressure (though mgmt cites fragmented client base reduces single-client leverage). 4) Ramp-up period costs for new facilities impacting short-term margins.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: 1) Shift from horizontal to vertical quick commerce as the primary growth lever, with Shadowfax positioning as the natural 3PL for capital-constrained vertical players. 2) AI is not just an efficiency tool but a demand generator by lowering technical barriers for SMEs to go online. 3) Network design philosophy: Fewer, larger last-mile nodes to optimize transportation mesh, contrary to industry trend of hyper-fragmented nodes. 4) Dual-running costs for 6-8 months per new facility create a temporary margin drag that masks true steady-state profitability.

commitments.title: Promises (RHP)
commitments.body:
- **Continue to expand the portfolio of clients and services as part of growing the value-velocity-versatility proposition.**
- **Strengthen and expand the logistics network and continue to invest in technology.**
- **Strategically expand vehicle leasing for cost-effective logistics operations.**
- **Expand the business internationally beyond India.**
- **Pursue strategic investment opportunities; the acquisition of 89.59% of Criticalog India Private Limited (agreement dated November 22, 2024) adds freight management, air/road express, freight forwarding, warehousing, customs clearance and …**
- **Management expects operating expenses to increase as growth initiatives are pursued, and the company may continue to experience losses and negative cash flows in the future.**
- **Promote EV and bicycle usage on the platform (two-wheeler EV rental marketplace, OEM partnerships); in H1 FY26 an average of 23.62% of hyperlocal delivery orders per month were completed using EVs or bicycles (baseline to track).**
- **Raise a Fresh Issue of Equity Shares aggregating up to Rs 10,000.00 million (alongside an Offer for Sale of Rs 9,072.69 million from which the company receives no proceeds).**

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Four stated strategic growth engines - Quick Commerce, Prime, Prime Large and CriticaLog - complementing the existing express and hyperlocal leadership and letting the company serve everything from rapid last-mile delivery to specialised high-value logistics.
- Quick commerce: consolidate leadership as India's leading third-party logistics provider for quick commerce, having validated the dark store operating model in FY 26 and laid the foundation to scale to 100+ dark stores in FY 27, while expanding across vertical quick commerce platforms and the newly commenced Amazon Now …

challenges.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers
challenges.body:
| Challenge | Beneficiary/Loser | Dir | Conviction | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rapid shift of SME/D2C sellers to online channels requiring reliable, high-margin logistics partners. | Shadowfax Technologies | beneficiary | High | Direct access to 15-16 lakh SMEs via Shadowfax 360 offers 15-20% higher realization than enterprise contracts; first-mover advantage in vertical QC dark stores. |
| Horizontal quick commerce players facing margin pressure and needing flexible, asset-light fulfillment partners. | Quick Commerce Platforms (Unlisted) | beneficiary | Med | Shadowfax's onboarding of Amazon Now and focus on vertical QC provides scalable infrastructure without capex burden for platforms. |
| Inefficient traditional 3PLs losing market share to consolidated, tech-enabled players. | Traditional/Fragmented 3PLs | loser | High | Shadowfax gaining 28-29% 3PL market share (up from 17-18% YoY) primarily at the expense of inefficient players and insourced arms. |

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Acquisition/integration] "CriticaLog integration and unprecedented demand for dark stores driving sustained growth momentum in Other Logistics" — the deck names CriticaLog only in this context and gives no consideration, date or ownership detail.
- [Key client] "Amazon Now ramping up ahead of plan" with "Rapid wallet share gains", and the deck notes "E-commerce players entering Quick-commerce are choosing 3PL for significant share of volumes"; Prime Large has "Onboarded one of India's largest horizontal E-com" (unnamed).
- [Seasonality] The business is explicitly geared to a festive peak — "Gearing Up for a Strong October 2026 Festive Season" and "Investing Ahead of Peak Festive Demand" — so capex and capacity lead revenue rather than track it.
- [Corporate status] Shadowfax Technologies Limited, formerly Shadowfax Technologies Private Limited, CIN U72300KA2015PLC150324, registered in Bangalore; listed on BSE (Scrip Code 544685) and NSE (Symbol SHADOWFAX).
- [Reporting basis] The deck reports two EBITDA measures side by side — Ind AS EBITDA of ₹92 Cr (6.8% margin) and Adjusted EBITDA of ₹67 Cr (4.9% margin) for Q1 FY27 — the bridge being share-based payments, Ind AS 116 lease-accounting rent adjustment and a one-time RTS cancellation item; the two must not be read as the same metric.
